subject: Creativity
title: CPS: Creative Problem Solving Model
description: A quick, practical guide to CPS: Creative Problem Solving Model.

hook.text: Alex Osborn (who invented brainstorming) and Sidney Parnes built the most widely used creative problem-solving model.

buildup.text: CPS has three stages: Clarify (understand the problem), Ideate (generate solutions), Develop (refine and plan action).

discovery.text: Its power is in 'Clarify.' Most people solve the wrong problem. CPS spends more time defining than solving.

twist.text: Osborn's original brainstorming rules are rarely followed: defer judgment, go for quantity, build on others' ideas.

climax.text: When CPS rules are actually followed, groups produce 2x more ideas and significantly more original solutions.

punchline.text: The inventor of brainstorming knew the rules. Everyone else forgot them.

quiz.question: What is the first stage of the CPS model?

details.summary: The Creative Problem Solving model structures the creative process into three stages: exploring the challenge, generating ideas, and preparing for action. Developed by Osborn and Parnes, CPS alternates between divergent and convergent thinking at each stage.
details.whyItMatters: CPS is the most widely used and researched creative process model. It provides a complete framework for moving from fuzzy problem to concrete action plan through deliberate creative thinking.
takeaways: CPS has three main stages each with divergent and convergent phases
It was developed by Alex Osborn and Sidney Parnes
The model separates idea generation from idea evaluation

faq.question: How does CPS differ from design thinking?
faq.answer: CPS focuses specifically on creative idea generation and problem framing. Design thinking adds user empathy research, prototyping, and testing. CPS is the underlying creative thinking engine that design thinking incorporates into a broader innovation process.

faq.question: Can individuals use CPS or is it only for groups?
faq.answer: CPS works for both individuals and groups. The divergent-convergent rhythm is a thinking discipline that anyone can apply alone. Groups benefit from the structured alternation between generating and evaluating ideas.
